passage: Kalyani stood by the grain bin in their house near Warangal, pointing at the top shelf. "Bi! Bi!" Her grandmother Chandrika, peeling a banana for her, held it out. "Here, bangaram, banana." Kalyani shoved the banana away so hard it fell on the floor. She sat down and cried, still pointing at the shelf where the biscuit tin lived. Chandrika picked up the banana and sighed.

qa.q: What was Chandrika peeling?
qa.a: She was peeling a banana for Kalyani.

qa.q: What was Kalyani feeling when she shoved the banana away?
qa.a: She was angry and upset because she wanted a biscuit, not a banana.

qa.q: What else could Chandrika try next time?
qa.a: She could ask Kalyani to point or show her what she wants before offering something, so the request is clear from the start.

qa.q: How does the moment feel for Chandrika?
qa.a: She is tired and a little disappointed that her offer was refused so sharply, and sighs as she picks it up.

grounding: A toddler set on a biscuit pushes away the banana she is offered and cries, because her goal was fixed and her request unclear.

passage: In the Berlin flat, Siddiq tugged at Olga's sleeve and said, "Cookie." Olga, his nanny, was stirring soup and heard "...ee". She peeled a banana and crouched down. "Banana! Yummy!" Siddiq's face crumpled. He pushed the banana back into her hand and wailed, "Cookie! Cookie!" He stamped once, then sat on the floor sobbing, pointing toward the cupboard where the cookie box stood.

qa.q: What was Olga stirring?
qa.a: She was stirring soup.

qa.q: What was Siddiq feeling when his face crumpled?
qa.a: He was disappointed and angry that he got a banana instead of the cookie he wanted.

qa.q: What would help Olga understand Siddiq better?
qa.a: Asking him to show her or point before she chooses, since the word got lost while she was cooking.

qa.q: How does the banana look to Siddiq?
qa.a: To Siddiq it is the wrong answer to a clear wish, so it feels like not being understood at all.

grounding: A toddler who wants a cookie is offered a banana, pushes it away and cries because his goal is fixed and his request was not clear.

passage: Freya had cried for a biscuit for a long time in the Copenhagen kitchen. Her father, Oskar, sat on the floor holding out a banana. "No biscuits before dinner, but this is here." Freya hiccupped, wiped her nose on her sleeve and looked at the banana. Her tummy rumbled. She reached out, took it with both hands and bit the end, peel and all. Oskar laughed and helped her peel it.

qa.q: What did Oskar hold out?
qa.a: He held out a banana.

qa.q: What was Freya feeling when she looked at the banana?
qa.a: She was still sad about the biscuit but hungry enough to change her mind.

qa.q: What went well in the way Oskar handled it?
qa.a: He waited calmly and kept offering the banana without scolding, so Freya could switch when she was ready.

qa.q: How does the change look to Oskar?
qa.a: Oskar sees her hunger win out and feels relieved, laughing and helping her peel it.

grounding: After crying for a biscuit, a toddler looks at the banana she is offered and takes it, changing her plan to getting any food.

passage: My name is Ramesh, and I share the flat with Charu's family. On Sunday Charu cried for biscuits, big wet cries, while her mother held out a banana. I kept reading. After a while the crying got smaller. Charu sniffed, stared at the banana, and slowly reached for it. She ate it all. I don't know if she changed her mind or was just too hungry to wait.

qa.q: What did Charu's mother hold out?
qa.a: She held out a banana.

qa.q: What was Ramesh thinking as the crying got smaller?
qa.a: Ramesh was curious and unsure, wondering whether Charu changed her mind or was just too hungry to wait.

qa.q: What small step helped Charu, and why?
qa.a: Her mother stayed calm and kept offering the banana, giving Charu time to take it.

qa.q: What might it be like for Charu when she takes the banana?
qa.a: She probably feels relief once her hunger is met, even though it isn't the biscuit.

grounding: An observer watches a toddler stop crying for a biscuit and take a banana instead, as hunger changes what she wants.

passage:
"How tall, Vaibhav?" Vandana asked from the sewing machine.
"Up to the table!" He set down a blue block, then red, then another.
"Four... five..." she counted.
The sixth block went on and the whole tower tipped over.
"Oh no!"
Vaibhav didn't answer. He started again: red at the bottom this time, then blue.
"New order?"
"Just trying," he said.

qa.q: At which block did the tower tip over?
qa.a: It tipped over when the sixth block went on.

qa.q: What was Vaibhav feeling when the tower fell?
qa.a: He seemed calm and determined rather than upset, starting again without a word.

qa.q: What else could Vaibhav try besides changing the order?
qa.a: He could put the biggest blocks at the bottom on purpose, because a wide base is steadier than a random order.

qa.q: How does Vaibhav's rebuilding look to Vandana?
qa.a: Vandana finds it interesting and supportive to watch, asking about his new order and letting him get on with it.

grounding: A child's tower falls at the sixth block, and he simply rebuilds it with the blocks in a slightly different order.

passage:
Note for Yogesh's mother, Dilnaz
Today in free play Yogesh built a tower with the wooden blocks. It fell when he added the sixth block. He looked at the pile for a second, then built it again, but swapped the bottom two. It fell at six again. He tried a third order. I did not step in; he seemed happy to keep testing.

qa.q: What did Yogesh swap on his second try?
qa.a: He swapped the bottom two blocks.

qa.q: What was Yogesh feeling as he kept rebuilding?
qa.a: He seemed happy and curious, keen to keep testing rather than frustrated.

qa.q: What else could help Yogesh get past six blocks?
qa.a: Noticing which blocks make a wider base and putting them lowest, since changing the order at random may not fix the wobble.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz feel reading the note?
qa.a: Dilnaz would likely feel pleased that Yogesh is persistent and that the note-writer let him explore.

grounding: A teacher's note describes a child rebuilding a fallen tower in slightly different orders by trial and error.

passage: Indu sat on the floor of the Pune flat, blocks spilled around her. "First the fat ones," she whispered, lining up the big square blocks. "Then the thin ones." She stacked the small cubes on top. "Then the flag." She stuck a paper flag on a toothpick and planted it in the top. Her uncle Tarun leaned in. "Who taught you that plan?" Indu shrugged. "Me."

qa.q: What did Indu plant at the top?
qa.a: A paper flag on a toothpick.

qa.q: What was Indu feeling when she answered "Me"?
qa.a: She was proud and confident that the plan was her own.

qa.q: What else could Indu add to her plan?
qa.a: She could add a check, like pressing the bottom blocks to see if they wobble, before putting on the flag.

qa.q: How does Indu's plan look to Tarun?
qa.a: Tarun is impressed and curious, surprised that she made up the steps herself.

grounding: A child talks herself through a simple ordered plan, big blocks, then small, then a flag, and builds in that order.

passage:
"What are you building, Lakshmi?" Preeti asked, sitting down with her own blocks.
"A temple. First the big blocks. For the floor."
"Then?"
"Then small ones. Then the flag on top." Lakshmi tapped each block as she spoke.
"Can I use the flag?"
"No, the flag is last. I need it at the end."
"You're so bossy."
Lakshmi smiled and set the flag aside.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi building?
qa.a: She was building a temple.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi thinking when she set the flag aside?
qa.a: She felt sure and determined about her order, wanting the flag saved for the end.

qa.q: What else could Lakshmi do so Preeti joins in?
qa.a: She could give Preeti a step in the plan, like the small blocks, so they build together.

qa.q: How does Lakshmi's plan look to Preeti?
qa.a: Preeti finds it bossy and is a bit annoyed that she can't have the flag.

grounding: A child says her building steps aloud, big blocks, then small, then the flag, and keeps to the order.

passage: Ramesh watched Arohi from the next flat build with the long wooden blocks. She laid two long ones side by side on the floor, then stacked on top. Her tower grew tall. Ramesh cleared away his wobbly one and set two long blocks flat, just like hers. He stacked. Seven, eight, nine. It stayed up. "Why?" his mother asked. Ramesh frowned and said, "It just does."

qa.q: What did Arohi lay side by side?
qa.a: She laid two long ones side by side on the floor.

qa.q: What was Ramesh feeling when his tower stayed up?
qa.a: He was probably pleased and surprised, though puzzled about why it worked.

qa.q: What could Ramesh's mother do to help him understand?
qa.a: She could let him try a narrow base next to a wide one, so he sees for himself why the wide one stands.

qa.q: How might Arohi feel seeing Ramesh copy her?
qa.a: Arohi might feel proud that her idea worked for him too, or mildly annoyed at being copied.

grounding: A boy copies a neighbour's wide base of two long blocks, and his tower goes higher though he cannot explain why.

passage:
"Aditi, how is yours so tall?" Siddharth asked across the play mat.
"I don't know. I just put these first." Aditi tapped two long blocks lying flat.
Siddharth copied, two long blocks, flat. Then he stacked. "Look! Mine's taller than before!"
"Why does it work?" asked Aditi.
"Because... it's long?" Siddharth shrugged. "It just does."

qa.q: What did Aditi put first?
qa.a: She put two long blocks lying flat.

qa.q: What was Siddharth feeling when he said "Look!"?
qa.a: He was excited and proud that his tower was taller than before.

qa.q: What would help Siddharth understand why it works?
qa.a: Building one tower on a narrow base and one on a wide base side by side, to see which wobbles.

qa.q: If you were Aditi, what would you think about being copied?
qa.a: You might feel pleased your idea helped, and curious because you can't explain it either.

grounding: A boy copies a friend's wide base of two long blocks and builds higher, without being able to explain why.

passage: At the preschool in Nagpur, Pradeep's tower was tall and narrow. "Stay up," he told it, patting the side. "And the red block goes on top. It's lucky." He placed it. The tower swayed. Vishal, next to him, said, "It's too thin at the bottom." "No," said Pradeep. "The red one's gone bad." He knocked the red block off and chose another.

qa.q: What did Pradeep say to the tower?
qa.a: He said, "Stay up."

qa.q: What was Pradeep thinking when he blamed the red block?
qa.a: He felt sure that luck, not the base, controls the tower, and was annoyed that the lucky block failed.

qa.q: What would you change first in Pradeep's tower?
qa.a: Make the bottom wider, as Vishal said, because a narrow base will sway whatever block goes on top.

qa.q: How does Pradeep's reasoning look to Vishal?
qa.a: Vishal can see the real problem and is probably frustrated that Pradeep won't listen.

grounding: A child relies on a lucky red block and telling the tower to stay up, then blames the block when it wobbles instead of the narrow base.

passage: I'm Vasudha, and I help at the community centre's play hour. Sonali built a thin tower and whispered to it, "Don't fall." Then she put the red block on top: "Red is my lucky colour." The tower wobbled. Sonali glared at the red block and said, "Naughty." She never looked at the narrow bottom. I wondered whether to say something, and decided to ask her a question instead.

qa.q: What did Sonali whisper to the tower?
qa.a: She whispered, "Don't fall."

qa.q: What was Vasudha feeling as she watched Sonali?
qa.a: Vasudha was unsure and thoughtful, torn between saying something and letting Sonali work it out.

qa.q: What question could Vasudha ask to help Sonali?
qa.a: She could ask, "What does the bottom look like?", which points Sonali to the base without giving the answer.

qa.q: What might the wobble be like for Sonali?
qa.a: She feels let down by her lucky block and blames it, which seems to her the obvious cause.

grounding: An observer watches a child rely on a lucky red block and blame it when the tower wobbles, not noticing the narrow base.

passage: The tower fell for the third time on the floor of Sarita's Lucknow flat. She sat back on her heels and stared at the scattered blocks. "It wobbles, and then it falls," she told her sister Jaya. "So if it wobbles... I make the bottom fatter." She laid four blocks wide at the bottom and started again. When the new tower swayed at the seventh block, she stopped, added two more at the base, and kept going.

qa.q: How many times had the tower fallen?
qa.a: It fell for the third time.

qa.q: What was Sarita feeling when she worked out her rule?
qa.a: She seemed thoughtful and hopeful, sure she had found a way to stop the falls.

qa.q: Which approach would you try if the fatter bottom still failed?
qa.a: Try slowing down and checking each block is flat and straight, since width is not the only reason towers sway.

qa.q: How might Jaya see Sarita's new rule?
qa.a: Jaya probably finds it clever and interesting to hear Sarita explain her plan out loud.

grounding: After three collapses, a child makes an if-then rule to widen the base when the tower wobbles, and uses it on the next tower.

passage:
"Again!" Neelam groaned as the tower fell.
"That's three times," said her cousin Chinmay.
"I know." She stared. "It always wobbles first. So... if it wobbles, I make the bottom wider."
"How wider?"
"More blocks at the bottom." She set five in a row.
Halfway up, it swayed. Neelam stopped, added two at the base. "See? Rule."
"Your rule works!"

qa.q: How many blocks did Neelam set in a row?
qa.a: She set five in a row.

qa.q: What was Neelam feeling when she said "See? Rule."?
qa.a: She felt proud and confident that her rule had worked.

qa.q: What else could Neelam add to her rule?
qa.a: She could also check that each block is placed straight, because a wide base won't fix blocks set crooked.

qa.q: How does Neelam's rule look to Chinmay?
qa.a: Chinmay is impressed and excited, saying her rule works.

grounding: After three falls, a child makes and tests the rule to widen the base when the tower wobbles.

passage:
Preschool note for Farhan's mother, Sangeeta
Farhan built his tower four times today. On the fourth fall he swept every block off the rug with his arm and said, "I hate this." He turned his back and folded his arms. I sat near him without talking for a while. Later we looked at the blocks together; he said the second tower had been the tallest, but he didn't want to try again today.

qa.q: What did Farhan say when he swept the blocks off?
qa.a: He said, "I hate this."

qa.q: What was Farhan feeling when he folded his arms?
qa.a: He was angry and discouraged after four falls.

qa.q: What would you advise for next time?
qa.a: Take a break after the second or third fall to calm down and look at what worked, like his second tower, before anger wipes the learning.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta feel reading this note?
qa.a: Sangeeta would likely feel sympathetic, and glad that someone sat with him calmly.

grounding: A preschool note describes a child who sweeps away his blocks in anger after the fourth fall, losing what earlier tries taught him.

passage: Rain drummed on the tin roof of the house in Shimoga as Hemant built his tower for the fourth time. His cousin Vaibhav watched. Three blocks, four, five, and down it went. Hemant's face went hot. He swept his arm across the mat and blocks flew into the corner. "I hate this!" He stomped to the door. Vaibhav said quietly, "Your third one was so tall, though."

qa.q: What did Hemant's cousin say quietly?
qa.a: He said, "Your third one was so tall, though."

qa.q: What was Hemant feeling when his face went hot?
qa.a: He was angry and frustrated after the tower fell for the fourth time.

qa.q: What could Hemant try instead of sweeping the blocks away?
qa.a: He could take a breath and look at what made the third tower tall, so the next try builds on that.

qa.q: How does the outburst look to Vaibhav?
qa.a: Vaibhav stays calm and wants to help, reminding Hemant of what worked.

grounding: A child sweeps away his blocks in anger after the fourth fall, and the learning from earlier towers is lost.

passage:
Saturday: Tanushree's tower kept falling. "Papa, hold the bottom?" Vikas pressed a finger on the lowest block while she stacked. She watched how he pushed each block square before letting go.
Monday: she asked again. This time she placed each block, then nudged it square like he did.
Wednesday: Papa was at work. Tanushree built alone, nudging every block straight. The tower stood tall.

qa.q: What did Vikas press on?
qa.a: He pressed a finger on the lowest block.

qa.q: What was Tanushree feeling when her tower stood tall on Wednesday?
qa.a: She was probably proud and happy that she did it alone using Papa's way.

qa.q: What else could Tanushree learn from Papa?
qa.a: She could ask him why square blocks stand better, so she understands the reason and not just the move.

qa.q: How might Vikas feel hearing about Wednesday's tower?
qa.a: Vikas would likely feel proud that she learned from watching him and now builds alone.

grounding: Over several days a child asks her father to hold the bottom block, watches how he sets blocks square, and later copies it building alone.

passage: The power cut came halfway through Siami's tower in the Aizawl flat, and the room went grey. The blocks kept sliding. "Pa, can you hold the bottom one?" Her father came with a torch, set it on the floor and held the base steady. Siami watched how he lined up each edge with his thumb. When the lights came back, she built another alone, lining every edge with her thumb.

qa.q: What did Siami's father bring?
qa.a: He came with a torch.

qa.q: What was Siami feeling when she asked for help?
qa.a: She was probably frustrated by the sliding blocks and hopeful that Pa could help.

qa.q: What else could Siami try if her father isn't there?
qa.a: She could use something flat as a guide or keep lining edges as he showed, since she already copied his thumb trick.

qa.q: How might Siami's father see her building alone later?
qa.a: He would likely feel proud that she watched him and used his method by herself.

grounding: A child asks her father to hold the bottom block during a power cut, watches how he lines up edges, and copies it when building alone.

passage:
"Ready or not!" Sangeeta shouted from the stairs.
Right at the centre of the living room, Ujjwal, who was four, clapped both hands over his eyes.
"Where's Ujjwal?" Sangeeta called, walking right up to him.
"You can't see me!"
"Um... I can see you."
"No! My eyes are closed!"
Sangeeta giggled and poked his tummy. "Found you."
"No fair!"

qa.q: Where was Ujjwal hiding?
qa.a: Right at the centre of the living room.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal thinking when he said "You can't see me!"?
qa.a: He was sure and happy that covering his eyes hid him, and felt it was unfair when he was found.

qa.q: What could Sangeeta do to help Ujjwal hide better?
qa.a: She could show him a spot behind the curtain and explain that she sees him even when his eyes are closed.

qa.q: How does the game look to Sangeeta?
qa.a: Sangeeta finds it funny and sweet, giggling because he is in plain view.

grounding: A four-year-old covers his eyes in the middle of the room and believes nobody can see him, not yet taking the seeker's view.

passage:
Kindergarten note for Gurpreet's parents, from Sabina
At hide-and-seek, Gurpreet, four, stood at the centre of the carpet with both hands over her eyes and whispered, "I'm hiding." The seeker walked straight to her. She was surprised to be found. Later I stood behind the door and asked, "Can you see me?" She thought, then went to hide behind the shelf.

qa.q: Where did Gurpreet stand to hide?
qa.a: At the centre of the carpet.

qa.q: What was Gurpreet feeling when the seeker found her?
qa.a: She was surprised and maybe a bit confused, since she believed covering her eyes kept her hidden.

qa.q: What worked well in Sabina's response?
qa.a: Letting Gurpreet feel what it's like to look for someone helped her see the seeker's view and move behind the shelf.

qa.q: What would change for the seeker if Gurpreet hid behind the shelf?
qa.a: The seeker would actually have to search, which makes the game more fun for them.

grounding: A teacher's note describes a four-year-old who covers her eyes on the carpet and thinks she is hidden, then learns to hide behind something.
